introduction: Why is the world not all of one kind? The guide answers that the order and perfection of the universe require difference: of kingdoms, of species, of capacities, colours and minds, all arising from one matter and one source. It distinguishes the difference that adorns from the difference that destroys, and it uses the garden, the meal of many dishes and the body with its members as its images. Its forty-eight quotations are read here with forty-eight from elsewhere. Paul’s body in which the eye cannot do without the hand, the psalmist’s manifold works, the Qur’an’s fruits and hills and peoples of many hues watered with one water, Hopkins’s dappled things, Aristotle’s state that is by nature a plurality and Kallen’s orchestra all say that variety belongs to wholeness. Heraclitus, for whom war is father of all, and Tennyson’s nature red in tooth and claw stand where the guide speaks of conflict and of eaters and eaten; Plato’s citizens of gold and brass, where differences of nature become ranks; the story of Babel, where the variety of peoples is a scattering; and the Gita, where the guide rejects the return of souls.
questions: The guide says the perfection of the universe requires difference. What would be lost in a world, or a community, of one kind only?
It distinguishes differences that adorn from differences that destroy. How can one tell which kind a given difference is?
All creatures are eaters and eaten, the guide says, and Tennyson calls nature red in tooth and claw. Is conflict part of the order being praised?
Plato turns differences of nature into fixed ranks. What keeps the teaching that people differ in capacity from being used in that way?
Babel tells the variety of peoples as a scattering, and the Qur'an says peoples were made different so as to know one another. Which story do you live by?
Blake says one law for the lion and the ox is oppression. What does fairness require where people genuinely differ?

outside.why: Paul asks: if the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing? and says the eye cannot tell the hand, I have no need of thee.
Pope pictures existence as a vast chain of being, from God through angel, man, beast, bird, fish and insect.
Kallen compares a society to an orchestra in which every type of instrument has its own timbre and tonality.
Heraclitus says that war is the father of all and the king of all. Can the difference that causes annihilation be so cleanly separated from the difference that is the mark of perfection?
The psalmist exclaims: O Lord, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all.
Genesis has the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle and creeping thing and beast.
Paul says that there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.
Aristotle says that the nature of a state is to be a plurality, and that too great a unity would destroy it.
The Qur'an points to fruits of divers hues, and to streaks white and red in the hills, of divers hues.
The Qur'an counts the difference of languages and colours among the signs of God.
Hopkins gives glory to God for dappled things, for skies of couple-colour and rose-moles all in stipple upon trout.
The Qur'an points to vineyards and date-palms, like and unlike, which are watered with one water.
Paul says that there is one glory of the sun and another of the moon, and that one star differeth from another star in glory.
Darwin contemplates an entangled bank clothed with many plants of many kinds, all produced by laws acting around us.
Aristotle observes that nature proceeds little by little from lifeless things to animal life.
Emerson says that all are needed by each one, and that nothing is fair or good alone.
Tennyson sees Nature red in tooth and claw, shrieking against the creed of love. Is a fabric of life reared on eaters and eaten part of the perfection of the universe, or a difficulty for it?
Shelley says that nothing in the world is single: all things by a law divine in one spirit meet and mingle.
Plato's Timaeus watches the elements pass into one another and compose the things we see.
The Preacher watches generations come and go, the sun rise and set, and the wind turn about continually.
Plato distinguishes what always is and has no becoming from what is always becoming and never is.
Lavoisier found that in every operation an equal quantity of matter exists before and after.
Leibniz says that each simple substance has relations which express all the others, and is a living mirror of the universe.
Dante ends his poem with the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
Paul says that the body is one and has many members, and all the members are one body.
The Rig Veda says that to what is One, sages give many a title.
The Chandogya Upanishad says that by one clod of clay all that is made of clay is known, the difference being only a name.
The Qur'an says that the heavens and the earth were of one piece, and were parted.
Job calls all that he has described only parts of God's ways.
The psalm says that by the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them.
The Gita pictures the spirit laying by worn-out robes and taking new ones. What does the guide put in the place of a soul's return in other forms?
The Preacher says that to every thing there is a season, a time to plant and a time to pluck up.
The psalm says that man flourishes as a flower of the field, and the wind passes over it and it is gone.
Acts says that God has made of one blood all nations of men.
The Preacher saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness.
In the parable talents are given to every man according to his several ability.
The Qur'an says even of the messengers that some have been caused to excel others.
Blake says that one law for the lion and ox is oppression. If creatures truly differ, what does equal treatment mean?

Plato's tale tells citizens that they are brothers, yet that God has framed them differently, some of gold and some of brass. When does a teaching about differences of nature become an excuse for fixed ranks?
The Qur'an says that humankind was made nations and tribes in order that they may know one another.
Genesis tells of one people with one language, scattered when their speech was confounded. Is the variety of peoples a gift, as the guide says, or a breaking, as that story tells it?
Pope says that whatever link is struck from nature's chain, tenth or ten thousandth, breaks the chain alike.
Paul says that we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office.
Whitman believes a leaf of grass no less than the journey-work of the stars, and the pismire equally perfect.
Paul says that those with gifts differing should each use the one given.
Adam Smith says that in civilized society a man stands at all times in need of the co-operation of great multitudes.
Marcus Aurelius says that all things from eternity are of like forms and come round in a circle.
The Qur'an says that God could have made humankind one community, but tries them by what he has given, and tells them to vie in good works. What is diversity of thought and character for?

corinthians-if-the-whole-body-were-an-ey.text: If the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing? If the whole were hearing, where were the smelling? But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him. And if they were all one member, where were the body? But now are they many members, yet but one body. And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you

ecclesiastes-wisdom-excelleth-folly.text: Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness

quran-fruits-of-divers-hues.text: Hast thou not seen that Allah causeth water to fall from the sky, and We produce therewith fruit of divers hues; and among the hills are streaks white and red, of divers hues, and (others) raven-black;

blake-one-law-for-the-lion-and-ox.text: One Law for the Lion & Ox is Oppression
